newsitem.title: CROATIA: Fate of Zagreb radio is a test case, diplomats say.
newsitem.headline: Fate of Zagreb radio is a test case, diplomats say.

text.p: The fate of an independent Zagreb radio which the authorities tried to shut down last week is a test case for Croatian democracy, diplomats said on Monday.
They warned that closing Radio 101 could be disastrous for the ruling nationalist HDZ party, whose popularity is rapidly declining ahead of presidential and local elections next year.
"Radio 101 is a test case of Croatia's commitment to democracy and we will keep monitoring the issue closely," a U.S. diplomat told Reuters.
The state-controlled Telecommunications Council gave Radio 101's frequency to a rival which does not yet exist in a move prompting unprecedented protests in Zagreb.

Over 100,000 people gathered in the capital's main square last Thurdsay to voice their support for the radio which has championed freedom of speech in Croatia and frequently attacked the right wing government.
When the United States and several Western governments issued warnings to Zagreb, the authorities agreed to reconsider.

"Croatia is at crossroads. The government and the people believe they are part of the West. But to be part of the West you must behave like the West. You must have a free press..," said the U.S. diplomat.
"There are certain standards of democracy that will determine the extent (of Croatia's integration)," he said.
President Franjo Tudjman, who has a reputation as an autocrat, appeared to brush off Western reprimands when he returned to Zagreb on Saturday after medical treatment in Washington.

"Croatian democracy will secure human rights for minorities, as well as freedom of the media. We will not allow solutions to be imposed (on us) from the outside... from countries unable to solve their own problems," he said.
Another Western diplomat said Tudjman's attitude could deter support from potential voters.
"It's looking like a confrontation between the Croatian population and the President and his ruling party," the diplomat said.
"He had a chance to tone it down but, judging by what he said, it looks as if there is going to be a confrontation. Another failure to grant (the radio) concession would spark off strong feelings."

U.S. sources claimed the 74-year-old president was treated in the United States for stomach cancer and was seriously ill but Croatian media played down his symptoms which were described as digestive problems.
